name: Subcision

lead: Subcision is a minor procedure in which a needle is inserted beneath the skin to cut the fibrous bands tethering a depressed scar, most often rolling acne scars. The payoff is a smoother skin surface as the scar lifts.

Releasing the scar creates a pocket where blood collects and collagen forms, which proponents say raises the scar. The term was coined in a 1995 paper describing a tri-beveled hypodermic needle. Studies include case series and small trials, and reviews list it within multimodal acne scar treatment.

paras: A clinician numbs the area and works the needle beneath each scarred zone, often in a series of sessions and combined with other scar treatments such as lasers or microneedling. Swelling and bruising settle over days, and collagen-related improvement is judged over following weeks to months.

Procedure-specific risks are not detailed in the sources reviewed, though bruising and swelling are expected from needle work under the skin. Medical sources describe subcision as in-office; do-it-yourself versions circulate in forums, where claims about results are anecdotal.

angle.text: Subcision is a clinic procedure that releases the fibrous bands pulling down rolling acne scars, so they lift and the skin surface looks smoother. Evidence consists of case series and small trials.

lead: Subcision is a minor in-office procedure in which a needle or blunt cannula is passed beneath the skin to cut the fibrous bands that hold a depressed scar down, most often rolling acne scars. Once released, the scar can rise toward the level of the surrounding skin, which is how people use it to smooth the texture of the face. The term was coined in a 1995 paper by Orentreich and Orentreich describing a tri-beveled hypodermic needle introduced through a small puncture, hence "incisionless" surgery [1][2].

Proponents say the release does two things: it lifts the tethered scar, and the small controlled injury under it prompts new collagen to form and support the lifted area. Published work on subcision for acne scars consists mainly of case series, split-face trials and small randomized studies, and general reviews place it within multimodal scar treatment alongside lasers, peels, microneedling and fillers [3][4][5][6]. The same technique has also been studied for cellulite dimples and for some wrinkles [7][8].

In looksmaxxing communities, subcision is discussed under skin texture ("skinmaxxing") as the step for scars that stay sunken when the skin is stretched, and it is frequently described as something done before or alongside laser or microneedling [9][10]. Dermatology sources describe it as a clinician-performed procedure, and a do-it-yourself version circulates on forums [9][11].
infobox: Rolling and tethered depressed acne scars [1][6]

Often repeated several times, at least 4 weeks apart [6]

paras: Atrophic acne scars are conventionally sorted into icepick, boxcar and rolling types [1]. Rolling scars are broad with a wave-like profile, and they are tethered by fibrous bands that pull the skin down toward deeper layers. Subcision is aimed at those bands: a needle is inserted horizontally under the scar and moved so that its edge cuts the fibres holding the skin down [2][6].

The Wikipedia article on scars lists subcision as a way of separating tissue to level deep rolling acne scars, often followed by laser, microdermabrasion or chemical peels [12]. Healthline describes it as suited to depressed scars rather than raised hypertrophic or keloid scars, and notes that people with active acne, infections, clotting disorders or those taking oral retinoids may be advised against it [6].

The review of cellulite subcision on PubMed Central gives the general rationale in a body-contouring setting: the procedure releases the reticular dermis from fibrous septal bands in subcutaneous fat, and the depression is treated only where it is visible at rest [13].

The 1995 Dermatologic Surgery paper introduced the name subcision for undermining depressed scars and wrinkles from beneath, using a tri-beveled hypodermic needle through a puncture [2]. Grokipedia attributes the work to David and Norman Orentreich [11].

Brazilian dermatologists extended the idea to cellulite: a series covering January 1995 to January 1998 treated 232 women aged 18 to 52 with cellulite on the thighs and buttocks by subcision and was published in 2000 [7].

For acne scars, a 2005 report by Alam, Omura and Kaminer developed a standard technique and followed 40 patients with rolling scars [14]. Since then, trials have tested variations in instruments (sharp needle, blunt cannula, radiofrequency or laser energy, vacuum assistance) and add-on treatments such as suction, platelet-rich plasma, hyaluronic acid and threads [15][16][17].

A 2023 review of instrumentation searched studies from 2000 to June 2022 that used subcision alone for acne scars. It included 17 articles covering 417 patients: 155 treated with sharp subcision, 235 with blunt instruments and 27 with energy-assisted devices. The authors reported that all instrument types were effective and that redness and swelling were common to all [16].

A review of clinical trials covering 16 articles found four that compared blunt cannula subcision with needle subcision; efficacy was comparable, while the cannula was associated with fewer side effects and higher patient satisfaction [17].

Energy-assisted versions are also studied. A split-face randomized trial compared radiofrequency-assisted subcision with conventional subcision in 17 completers; both sides improved and scores from blinded assessors were similar, though patients rated the radiofrequency side better. Two small entry-point burns on that side healed within a month, and one persistent hematoma occurred on the conventional side [18]. In body treatment, vacuum-assisted and laser-assisted devices are used for cellulite subcision [13].

The 2005 study of 40 patients with rolling scars reported about 50 percent improvement by both patient and investigator ratings at six months, with 90 percent of patients saying their appearance had improved. Swelling, bruising and pain were temporary, though persistent firm bumps could occur at treatment sites. The authors suggested that combining subcision with other procedures or repeating it might help scars that do not fully resolve [14].

A 2008 trial in 22 patients (20 completed) with rolling scars compared subcision alone with subcision plus an absorbable catgut implant on opposite sides of the face. About 60 percent showed mild and about 40 percent moderate improvement, the implant made no significant difference, and side effects of edema, bruising and infection were transient [19].

A 2024 split-face randomized study in five patients with rolling scars gave one side five subcision sessions four weeks apart and left the other untreated. The treated side showed a greater fall in global scarring score by week 36, and half of the patients preferred the treated side [20]. Another 2024 split-face trial compared one subcision followed by ten suction sessions on one side with subcision alone: blinded dermatologists found no difference, but participants preferred the combination at one and four months [21].

A 2014 protocol that began with a single subcision and then alternated microneedling and a trichloroacetic acid peel (after tretinoin priming) reported that all 49 completers improved by at least one grade and that rolling, boxcar and linear tunnel scars responded while ice pick scars changed little or not at all. Because subcision was combined with other treatments, its separate contribution cannot be isolated, as the authors note [22].

Reviews describe the overall literature candidly. A 2019 review of acne scar treatments noted few high-quality studies, a variety of severity scales and frequently undefined scar types, which makes trials hard to compare [4]. A 2023 evidence review rated lasers, platelet-rich plasma, peels, fillers and microneedling as having stronger support and described subcision as having lower-quality evidence [23]. A 2023 review of subcision trials concluded it is safe and effective for atrophic acne scars and that modifications and combinations may improve results [17].

The 2000 cellulite series reported in its abstract that subcision was useful for advanced-grade cellulite [7]. The PubMed Central review describes a retrospective series of 232 patients with 78.87 percent satisfaction after one treatment, with results persisting at two years in the 23 patients followed that long; it also describes painful bruising and hemosiderin pigmentation lasting months and notes that the series lacked objective grading criteria [13].

A 2019 review of cellulite treatments lists acoustic wave therapy, subcision and a 1440 nm minimally invasive laser among the options with the most benefit [24], and a 2023 roundtable review notes that bruising is typical for treatments targeting fibrous septa, such as subcision, and can in some cases leave lasting pigmentation [25]. The original 1995 paper also described use on wrinkles [2].

Reported effects are mainly local. The trials above describe swelling, bruising, pain and redness, usually settling in one to two weeks [14][19][6]. Persistent firm bumps at treatment sites were noted in the 40-patient series [14], and a persistent hematoma was seen in one patient in a split-face trial [18].

Healthline lists infection, skin discoloration and injury to nearby nerves or blood vessels as less common effects, and says treatment is often repeated three to six times at least four weeks apart [6]. Grokipedia states that hyperpigmentation is more likely in darker skin and that nerve damage is a concern mainly in facial work; it also says few studies include darker skin types [11].
Wikipedia's article on scars cautions more generally that scarring varies with skin type and that treatments for keloid-prone patients need care [12].

On looksmax.org, subcision appears in skin-texture threads as an option for scars that remain sunken when the surrounding skin is stretched. One thread by a user promoting the procedure describes it as a way to release the scar so skin rises and collagen is triggered, with lasers or peels afterward [10]. A long guide posted by another user presents a do-it-yourself approach, including a self-test for tethering [9].

Replies in the threads describe subcision as a late-stage option after microneedling and laser, and some posters say it improved their texture and is under-discussed because of worries about sagging [9]. Dermatology sources and reviews describe the procedure as performed by clinicians under local anesthetic [6][16].

Human studies include a 2005 case series of 40 patients [14], a 2008 split-face catgut-implant trial [19], a 2020 radiofrequency-assisted split-face randomized trial [18], 2024 split-face randomized trials of multiple subcisions and of subcision with suction [20][21], a stromal vascular fraction trial [26], and a pilot study of endo-radiofrequency subcision in 30 patients [27]. A review of 16 trials and a review of 17 instrumentation studies summarize this body of work [16][17].

Registered trials compare subcision with or alone against CO2 laser, platelet-rich plasma, exosomes, suction, cannula versus needle technique, and other combinations [15][28][29][30], and cellulite studies exist [31][32].

lore.intro: Subcision is discussed on looksmax.org as a skin-texture step for tethered atrophic scars, usually after gentler treatments, and a DIY version is debated [9][10].

claims.claim: Subcision works for tethered scars better than microneedling or laser.
If a scar does not flatten when you pull the skin, it is tethered and suited to subcision.
It can be done at home.
Subcision triggers collagen release that keeps improving texture.
Subcision is a last resort, tried after other treatments fail.
Worries that subcision causes facial sagging are overstated.
Combining subcision with suction or other add-ons gives a better result.

timeline.event: Subcision described and named in Dermatologic Surgery as a way to correct depressed scars and wrinkles [2].
Patients in a Brazilian cellulite series (n=232) treated by subcision; published in 2000 [7].
Acne scar classification (icepick, boxcar, rolling) and treatment review published, giving the field a shared vocabulary [1].
Technique and outcomes reported in 40 patients with rolling acne scars [14].
Split-face trial of subcision with or without catgut implant in 20 patients [19].
Combination protocol beginning with subcision, then microneedling and TCA peels, reported in 49 patients [22].
Multimodality approach tailored to scar type published in Dermatologic Surgery [5].
Randomized split-face trial of radiofrequency-assisted versus conventional subcision [18].
Reviews of subcision trials and of subcision instrumentation published [16][17].
Split-face randomized trials of multiple subcisions and of subcision with suction published [20][21].
